description: A square backdrop-filter: blur(8px) panel over colored shapes with nothing else on it: the blur must continue the colors up to the panel edge instead of fading toward the canvas, which is what the edge of a backdrop blur reads.

florui.css: .scene { position: relative; width: 200px; height: 140px; background-color: #1b1b2f; overflow: hidden; } .s1 { position: absolute; left: 10px; top: 10px; width: 90px; height: 90px; background-color: #ff5a5f; border-radius: 45px; } .s2 { position: absolute; left: 80px; top: 50px; width: 100px; height: 70px; background-color: #2ec4b6; } .s3 { position: absolute; left: 20px; top: 90px; width: 70px; height: 40px; background-color: #ffd166; } .glass { position: absolute; left: 40px; top: 30px; width: 120px; height: 80px; backdrop-filter: blur(8px); }

classification.reason: Chromium and this engine build a Gaussian blur differently (kernel shape and rounding), so a pixel in the blurred area differs by a few levels of 255 and a pixel at a steep colour edge by more. Measured against desktop Chrome: measured with the plain blur and no tint. channel_tolerance 8 stops the harmless rounding from counting; the percentage left is the steep edges. With the backdrop blur read past the panel edge as transparent instead of mirrored (the defect this fixture found), about 30% of the pixels differed by more than that.
